Mechanistic interpretability · Neograph project · May 2026

The grammar-suppression layer

Half a dozen language models — from EleutherAI's tiny Pythia 70M up to Mistral 7B and Gemma 2 9B — can all finish "The capital of France is" with " Paris." Open them up and each one is leaning on roughly the same ten internal features per prompt. Take those ten features away and every model breaks. But only one of them is fighting itself to get there.

Loading data…

Two ways a brain can finish a sentence

Cognitive neuroscience has spent two decades arguing about a basic structural question: when a brain does a task, does it light up task-specific regions (a visual region for seeing, a calculation region for arithmetic, an episodic region for remembering), or does it route everything through a shared general-purpose apparatus that just plugs in different content? The standard answer is "both". The content-specific systems are the task-positive networks. The general-purpose system is the multi-demand network — a handful of frontoparietal regions that light up whether you're doing mental arithmetic, language comprehension, or working-memory recall.

Run a functional scan on two language models — Gemma 2 2B (Google) and GPT-2 small (OpenAI, 2019) — answering the same 50 next-token prompts, and the cortical-routing question becomes concrete. The earlier version of this writeup claimed Gemma had a "multi-demand" routing strategy and GPT-2 didn't, based on what features participated in attribution circuits. The claim was directionally right and mechanistically wrong. What's actually going on is sharper, and stranger.

The setup, in plain English

  1. Pick a prompt the model is likely to complete correctly: "The capital of France is". Run it. Look at the model's last-layer residual stream right before it picks a next token.
  2. Decompose that residual stream into a sparse sum of ~16,000 labelled "concept features" via a pre-trained sparse autoencoder. Each feature comes with a plain-language label like "references to days of the week and their associated schedules" or "past and present tense forms of the verb 'to be'".
  3. For each active feature, do a counterfactual: zero it out, re-run the forward pass, watch how much the model's confidence in " Paris" changes. That gives you a per-feature causal contribution score.
  4. Sort by that score. The features with the biggest positive contribution are supporting: the model leans on them to pick the right answer. The features with the biggest negative contribution are opposing: they actively push probability mass away from the right answer.
  5. Test the supports. Take the top-10 supporting features. Zero them out all at once. If the model still finishes with " Paris", those ten weren't doing the work after all. If completion collapses, they were.

Run this on 52 prompts spanning 12 task categories — capitals, weekdays, math, named entities, code, reasoning chains, factual recall, pronoun resolution, syntactic completion, instruction-following, multi-step arithmetic, summarization openers. Then look at what kinds of features are doing what.

The headline: ten features hold up the prediction

Across every category, for every model tested, zeroing the per-prompt top-10 supporting features collapses hit rate to roughly zero. Target log-probability drops by 1–6 nats. The model breaks uniformly — capitals, weekdays, math, named entities, reasoning, all of it.

Why this matters. A working language model with billions of parameters will, on any given prompt, build its next-token prediction on a handful of features out of tens of thousands available. Find those ten, ablate them, and the prediction collapses — across every task category, in every model we tested. That's a much tighter bound on "where the work is happening" than the field usually gets.

Per-category breakdown (hit rate before → after, target log-prob drop)

The first surprise: supporting features are mostly content, not grammar

An earlier read of these models suggested they routed through a small "predicate backbone" of grammar features — "forms of to-be", "statements of existence", "the word 'is'". Those features fire on almost any prompt with a copula in it, so they showed up in attribution circuits for capitals, weekdays, math, named entities, you name it. Looked like a multi-demand network.

They're not load-bearing. Zero them out jointly and nothing happens — the model still gets " Paris", still gets " Tuesday", still gets " four". The real supporting set is a different cast of features per prompt, and they're almost all content-thematic:

Reading those lists, the model looks like it's running on task-positive networks: different content features for different domains, no shared grammar core. The original multi-demand framing was wrong.

The deeper surprise: grammar features are there, on the other side

Look at the opposing features — the ones whose ablation makes the correct answer more likely. Suddenly the missing grammar features show up. "Past and present tense forms of the verb 'to be'", "statements of existence", "instances of the word 'is'": they were never supporting " Paris" or " Tuesday". They were broadcasting probability across every plausible "X is Y" completion and, in doing so, suppressing the specific Y the model is meant to produce.

Quantitatively, across 52 prompts in Gemma 2 2B:

The "grammar layer" was never on the supporting side. It's on the suppression side. Multi-demand-network in form, suppressor-of-specifics in function.

The cross-model thing: Gemma has this. GPT-2 doesn't. Pythia 70M doesn't either.

Run the same analysis on three models of very different lineages — Gemma 2 2B (Google, 2024), GPT-2 small (OpenAI, 2019), Pythia 70M (EleutherAI, 2022) — and only Gemma exhibits the inversion. GPT-2 and Pythia both have load-bearing supporting features (their predictions collapse under joint ablation the same way), and their grammar share on the supporting side is similar to Gemma's. But on the opposing side, GPT-2's grammar share stays roughly equal to its supporting share, and Pythia's actually drops.

The original v2 cross-model claim — "Gemma routes through a grammar layer, GPT-2 doesn't" — was real, but it was on the wrong side of the equation. What Gemma 2 2B uniquely has, that GPT-2 small and Pythia 70M don't, is a layer of mid-late residual-stream features that suppress specific completions on declarative sentences. Call it a grammar-suppression layer.

When does the suppressor flip into a supporter?

The category texture matters. Gemma's grammar-suppression effect is strongest on tasks where the target is a specific noun-phrase fact after a copula: capitals (16× grammar enrichment on opposing vs supporting), weekdays (7.5×), code (6×), syntactic continuations (3×). For these, the model needs to push past generic "X is Y" alternatives to commit to a specific Y.

But for factual recall ("Water is composed of hydrogen and ___") and pronoun resolution ("After she finished shopping, ___"), the enrichment flips: grammar features show up on the supporting side, not the opposing side. For these, the target is a grammatical or referential element, so structural features help rather than hinder. Same features, opposite role, depending on what the target is.

So the "grammar layer" in Gemma's residual stream isn't either-or. It's role-bivalent — a single coordinated apparatus that supports the answer when the answer is structural and suppresses the answer when the answer is specific.

Why this matters

  • Attribution score ≠ load-bearing. The naive "find features that attribution-score highly across many tasks" recipe identified five Gemma features that look like a grammar backbone but contribute almost nothing to actual completion. Field-wide: any interpretability claim that rests on circuit participation breadth needs a causal joint-ablation cross-check.
  • Feature valence is a thing. Most SAE work treats features as either firing or not. The supporting/opposing distinction here shows that the same feature can be load-bearing in either direction, and the direction can be the whole story. The grammar features in Gemma have been hiding in plain sight as suppressors.
  • Suppression structure can be model-specific. Gemma 2 2B has a coordinated grammar-suppression apparatus that GPT-2 small and Pythia 70M lack. Three architecturally similar transformers, trained by different orgs on different data, ended up with structurally different inhibitory machinery in their residual streams. That's a hint that "what the model has learned to push down" varies more across training lineages than "what it has learned to push up."
  • The brain analogy is real but inverted. The earlier framing ("Gemma has a multi-demand network, GPT-2 doesn't") was directionally right — Gemma does have a content-invariant shared apparatus in its mid-late residual stream. It just happens to be wired for inhibition, not for promotion.

What this is not

  • A capability claim. Both models complete these prompts at non-trivial rates; this isn't about which is smarter.
  • A claim about every layer. We sample one canonical residual-stream SAE per model (Gemma layer 20, GPT-2 layer 8, Pythia layer 5). Other layers might tell a different story.
  • A claim about every prompt the model handles. 52 prompts is a start, not a complete sample of language.
  • A claim about generation. We only test next-token prediction. Multi-token generation likely recruits a different feature set per step.
  • A claim about causality between training data and routing strategy. We can show that the suppression layer exists; we can't yet show why Gemma's training produced it and others' didn't.
